execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: true editor: visual --- # Caveat emptor ## Caveats I will be showing you what you *can* do, not what you *should* do
. . . Creating LLM tools for phenotyping is relatively easy. Creating tools that are trusted, improve the quality of research, and provide a good user experience is the hard part.
. . . Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, or for which task.
. . . System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.
. . . Closed-weight cloud-based models show performance drift, making validation even harder. ## More caveats Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc)
. . . And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources) ## Even more caveats Low quality health research is prevalent
. . . Reproducibility crisis in health research
. . . LLM integration can go both ways. Increasing risk of OMOP-slop vs additional context and double-checking. # Working with LLMs from R ## ellmer We'll be using the `ellmer` R package for interacting with LLMs.
. . . Provides a simple interface for working with LLMs in a consistent manner.
. . . Building on `ellmer`, we can add model-agnostic support with users choosing the model to use. ## Unstructured chat `ellmer` supports various popular providers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- chat_anthropic() chat <- chat_deepseek() chat <- chat_google_gemini() chat <- chat_mistral() chat <- chat_openai() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_google_gemini() |> dplyr::pull("id") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "antigravity-preview-05-2026" [2] "antigravity-preview-09-2026" [3] "antigravity-preview-latest" [4] "deep-research-max-preview-04-2026" [5] "deep-research-preview-04-2026" [6] "deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025" [7] "gemini-2.5-computer-use-preview-10-2025" [8] "gemini-2.5-flash" [9] "gemini-2.5-flash-image" [10] "gemini-2.5-flash-lite" [11] "gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts" [12] "gemini-2.5-pro" [13] "gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts" [14] "gemini-3-flash-preview" [15] "gemini-3-pro-image" [16] "gemini-3-pro-image-preview" [17] "gemini-3.1-flash-image" [18] "gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview" [19] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite" [20] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image" [21] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview" [22] "gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview" [23] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview" [24] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools" [25] "gemini-3.5-flash" [26] "gemini-3.5-flash-lite" [27] "gemini-3.5-transcribe" [28] "gemini-3.6-flash" [29] "gemini-3.7-flash" [30] "gemini-3.8-flash" [31] "gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts" [32] "gemini-3.8-flash-tts" [33] "gemini-4-argon" [34] "gemini-flash-latest" [35] "gemini-flash-lite-latest" [36] "gemini-nano-banana-2.1" [37] "gemini-omni-1.1-flash" [38] "gemini-omni-flash-preview" [39] "gemini-pro-latest" [40] "gemini-robotics-er-2-preview" [41] "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it" [42] "gemma-4-31b-it" [43] "lyria-3-clip-preview" [44] "lyria-3-pro-preview" [45] "lyria-3.5" [46] "nano-banana-pro-preview" ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Similarly, we can run open-weight models locally via Ollama: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat <- chat_ollama() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_ollama() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id created_at size capabilities 1 MedGemma:4b 2026-10-14 3338942556 completion,vision 2 gemma3:4b 2026-10-14 3350272403 completion,vision 3 qwen2.5:0.5b 2026-10-14 397821319 completion,tools 4 gemma3:1b 2026-10-14 806067407 completion ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat I'm going to be using local MedGemma 4B today. You can choose a model you have access to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(dplyr) library(PhenotypeR) system_prompt <- "You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based." chat_medgemma <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) chat_medgemma ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ── system ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat We can work with a simple, unstructured, chat. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension is characterized by elevated blood pressure, typically defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥90 mm Hg. Clinical features include: * **Headaches, dizziness, blurred vision:** Due to cerebral hypoperfusion and increased intracranial pressure. * **Chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations:** Possible signs of cardiac complications (e.g., heart failure, coronary artery disease). * **Visual disturbances (amaurosis fugax):** Transient monocular blindness due to carotid artery stenosis. * **Peripheral neuropathy:** Nerve damage leading to numbness, tingling, and pain in extremities. * **Renal dysfunction:** Damage to the kidneys, potentially leading to chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease. * **Hypertensive encephalopathy:** Severe hypertension with neurological symptoms like headache, confusion, seizures, and coma. * **Cerebrovascular events (stroke):** Increased risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. * **Myocardial infarction:** Increased risk of heart attack * **Heart failure:** Increase risk of heart failure * **Peripheral artery disease (PAD):** Increased risk of PAD * **Sexual dysfunction:** Potential for erectile dysfunction in men, and reduced libido in both sexes. The clinical presentation of hypertension can range from asymptomatic to severe, life-threatening complications. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to reduce cardiovascular risk. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension is more prevalent in: * **Older adults:** Incidence increases with age. * **Men:** Generally, men have a higher prevalence of hypertension than women, especially in younger age groups. * **African Americans:** Higher prevalence compared to Caucasians and Asians. * **Individuals with a family history of hypertension.** * **Individuals with certain ethnicities/races:** as mentioned above. * **Individuals with certain health conditions:** such as diabetes, kidney disease, and sleep apnea. * **Individuals with certain socioeconomic statuses:** generally, lower socioeconomic status is associated with higher prevalence. * **Individuals with certain geographic locations:** some regions have higher prevalence due to lifestyle and environmental factors. The demographic distribution of hypertension can vary across different populations and settings. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Bad idea: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What clinical codes should I use to identify hypertension in my OMOP CDM?") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` To identify hypertension in your OMOP CDM, focus on relevant clinical codes, considering both diagnosis and procedure codes: * **ICD-10 Diagnosis Codes:** * I10 (Essential (Primary) Hypertension) * I11 (Secondary Hypertension) * I15 (Hypertensive Heart Disease) * I16 (Hypertensive Cardiovascular Disease) * I17 (Hypertensive Renal Disease) * I18 (Hypertensive Retinopathy) * I19 (Unspecified Hypertension) * **Procedure Codes (consider if applicable):** * May be relevant if hypertension was diagnosed during a specific procedure (e.g., cardiac catheterization). * **Medication Codes:** * Review medication codes for medications commonly used to treat hypertension (e.g., ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics, ARBs, calcium channel blockers). * **OMOP CDM Specifics:** * Utilize the OMOP CDM's standardized terminology for conditions (e.g., using the correct ICD-10 code). * Map to appropriate terms, considering potential variations in coding practices across different providers or institutions. * Be mindful of missing data and ensure consistent coding practices in your cohort. * The best codes depends on the specific dataset. Always check coding guidelines at your clinical sites. * **Considerations:** * In real-world data, coding practices can vary. Using a combination of diagnosis and procedure codes can provide a more comprehensive picture of hypertension. * Focus on the diagnosis codes first, then supplement with procedure codes as needed. * Review patient records to confirm accurate coding practices before including individuals in your cohort. * Use a tool like the OMOP CDM's automated coding capabilities for standardized coding practices ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Instead of allowing freedom in output, we can instead force results to be returned in a specific structured format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", type = type_object( typical_symptoms = type_string("summarise typical symptoms"), confirmatory_test = type_string("summarise what test result would confirm diagnosis"), disqualifying_diagnoses = type_string("summarise what alternative diagnoses need to be ruled out") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $typical_symptoms [1] "Headache, dizziness, blurred vision, chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, visual disturbances, peripheral neuropathy, renal dysfunction, hypertensive encephalopathy, cerebrovascular events (stroke), myocardial infarction, heart failure, or peripheral artery disease (PAD)." $confirmatory_test [1] "Blood pressure readings ≥140 mmHg systolic or ≥90 mmHg diastolic." $disqualifying_diagnoses [1] "Conditions that can mimic hypertension or are due to secondary causes (e.g., thyroid disease, sleep apnea). Consider defining your cohort carefully to exclude these. The exact criteria should be clearly defined before cohort definition and included in the study description." ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can force results to be integers/ numbers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension", type = type_object( average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("What is the average age at diagnosis?"), proportion_male = type_number("What proportion (between 0 and 1) of patients diagnosed with hypertension are male?") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $average_age_at_diagnosis [1] 63 $proportion_male [1] 0.53 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat But remember, even with the same model you can get different results! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 46 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 56 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 59 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 59 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 60 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 56 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = -10 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can set temperature to zero and add a seed to get closer to reproducibility. (This generally works better for local models than when working with cloud models.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt, params = params(temperature = 0, seed = 42) ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 ``` ::: ::: # Integrating LLMs with PhenotypeR ## Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models - Available to all of the OHDSI community
. . . - Smoother package development (easy to implement, cheaper, and straightforward to test)
. . . - Easy to switch to using frontier models (and see if they are worth the extra cost).
. . . - But 6+ months behind "state-of-the-art". (Although allows us to learn from experience of others) ## Human-in-the-loop - Designed to support the human phenotyper, not automate them away.
. . . - All LLM-generated artefacts can be inspected, reviewed, and edited.
. . . - Main use of LLM is to provide additional context making it easier to double-check results ## Phenotyping tasks > "A problem well stated is a problem half solved." > > Charles F. Kettering (1876 – 1958)
. . . Nowadays, a problem well stated is a problem 95% solved. ## Phenotyping tasks Started with lower-stakes, human-in-the-loop, phenotyping tasks: - Drafting clinical descriptions . . . - Reviewing codes included that led to cohort inclusion . . . - Contextualising PhenotypeR results . . . Higher-risk tasks currently out-of-scope: - Searching for codes. . . . - Creating cohort logic. . . . - End-to-end phenotyping # Clinical descriptions ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clinicalDescriptionSpecification() |> listviewer::jsonedit() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyClinicalDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, "hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for hypertension using MedGemma:4b ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $hypertension $hypertension$metadata $hypertension$metadata$phenotype_name [1] "hypertension" $hypertension$metadata$version [1] "1.0" $hypertension$metadata$created_by [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$metadata$created_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_by [1] "N/A" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$source_of_information [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$clinical_profile $hypertension$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms [1] "Hypertension is a chronic condition characterized by elevated blood pressure. Common synonyms include high blood pressure, arterial hypertension, and systemic hypertension." $hypertension$clinical_profile$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms [1] "Clinical presentation can be subtle, with many people experiencing no symptoms in the early stages. As hypertension progresses, symptoms may include severe headaches, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, dizziness, vision problems, and chest pain. Some people may experience a persistent feeling of fatigue." $hypertension$clinical_profile$assessment_diagnosis [1] "Assessment typically involves measuring blood pressure on multiple occasions. Diagnostic criteria for hypertension are established by professional medical organisations and include both systolic and diastolic blood pressure readings. Diagnostic tests also may involve further workup to discover if hypertension is secondary, such as measurement of aldosterone concentration, or imaging studies of the kidneys." $hypertension$clinical_profile$therapeutic_plan_treatment [1] "The initial treatment approach involves lifestyle modifications such as dietary changes, regular exercise, and weight management. If lifestyle changes are insufficient, medications may be prescribed. These may include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and alpha-blockers. The specific medication chosen depends on factors such as blood pressure readings, presence of other medical conditions, and individual patient characteristics. A healthcare professional will also monitor the patient's response to treatment and adjust the medications accordingly." $hypertension$clinical_profile$complications_prognosis [1] "Untreated or poorly controlled hypertension can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney failure, and heart failure. Short-term prognosis depends on the severity of hypertension and the presence of other medical conditions. Medium-term prognosis varies, with ongoing management and monitoring. Long-term prognosis depends on the effectiveness of treatment, lifestyle changes, and continued monitoring. Patients diagnosed with hypertension are advised to seek regular medical checkups and follow their doctor's recommendations." $hypertension$clinical_profile$disqualifiers [1] "Differential diagnoses to consider include white coat hypertension, secondary hypertension (caused by other medical conditions), and pseudo-hypertension (where blood pressure appears elevated but is not truly high). Patients presenting with sudden onset of severe hypertension, associated with other symptoms such as chest pain or shortness of breath, may require urgent investigation to rule out other medical conditions such as acute aortic dissection or acute myocardial infarction. If symptoms do not improve after a week of regular monitoring and lifestyle modifications, consider conditions such as preeclampsia/eclampsia, thyroid disorders, renal artery stenosis or medications that can raise blood pressure." $hypertension$clinical_profile$epidemiology [1] "Hypertension is more common in older adults. The prevalence and incidence of hypertension vary among different populations, with differences in lifestyle and genetics playing a role. Modifiable risk factors include high sodium intake, low potassium intake, obesity, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol consumption, and tobacco use. Non-modifiable risk factors include age, family history, race, and ethnicity. Common comorbidities associated with hypertension include cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney disease, and peripheral arterial disease." ``` ::: ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, c("Primary hypertension", "Secondary hypertension", "Resistant hypertension")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Primary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Primary hypertension is a chronic medical condition characterized by elevated blood pressure in the absence of a readily identifiable secondary cause. Other synonyms include essential hypertension, benign hypertension, and chronic hypertension. It is a major public health concern due to its association with increased cardiovascular risk." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Secondary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Secondary hypertension, resistant hypertension, secondary cause of hypertension, secondary hypertensive disorder, hypertensive emergency" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Resistant hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Resistant hypertension is defined as hypertension that remains uncontrolled despite the use of three antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic, at optimal doses, or the use of four medications, including two diuretics, at optimal doses. This condition is also referred to as difficult-to-control hypertension, refractory hypertension, or resistant hypertension." ``` ::: ::: ## Extra context: data source descriptions Data partner descriptions can be used to provide extra context ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyDataSourceDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: # Reviewing codes ## Reviewing codes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(omock) library(CohortConstructor) library(PhenotypeR) library(gt) cdm <- mockCdmFromDataset(datasetName = "synpuf-1k_5.4", source = "duckdb") cdm$hypertension <- conceptCohort(cdm, list(hypertension = c(320128, 312648, 201826, 313217)), name = "hypertension") code_diag <- codelistDiagnostics(cdm$hypertension) reviewCohortConcepts(chat_medgemma, code_diag, hypertension_cd) |> select(standard_concept, source_concept_name, score, explanation) |> gt() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Evaluation ## Benchmarking LLM performance We can use the `vitals` package to test how closely LLM output matches known clinical benchmarks. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(vitals) vitals::vitals_log_dir_set(tempdir()) age_benchmark <- tibble( input = "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", target = "50" ) score_within_5_years <- function(samples) { est_age <- purrr::map_int(samples$solver_metadata, "average_age_at_diagnosis") target_age <- as.integer(samples$target) list( score = factor( ifelse(abs(est_age - target_age) <= 5, "Pass", "Fail"), levels = c("Fail", "Pass"), ordered = TRUE ) ) } chat_medgemma_fresh <- chat_medgemma$clone() chat_medgemma_fresh$set_turns(list()) chat_medgemma_fresh$set_system_prompt(system_prompt) age_task <- Task$new( dataset = age_benchmark, solver = generate_structured( solver_chat = chat_medgemma_fresh, type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("Estimated average age in years") ) ), scorer = score_within_5_years ) age_task$eval(epochs = 10, view = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ℹ Solving ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [working] (0 + 0) -> 9 -> 1 But note we can't use them directly with structured chat. Here is a summary of the step-by-step approach to diagnosing hypertension: --- ### 1. Initial Clinic Blood Pressure (BP) Measurement * **Check the pulse first:** Palpate the radial or brachial pulse before measuring BP. If the pulse is irregular (suggesting atrial fibrillation), automated devices may be inaccurate—measure BP **manually** using direct auscultation over the brachial artery. * **Measure in both arms:** When considering a diagnosis, measure BP in both arms. If the difference in readings between arms is **more than 15 mmHg**, repeat the measurements. If the difference remains >15 mmHg on the second reading, use the arm with the **higher** reading for all subsequent measurements. * **Multiple readings in clinic:** If the first reading in the clinic is **≥ 140/90 mmHg**, take a second reading. If the second reading is substantially different from the first, take a third reading. **Record the lower of the last two measurements** as the clinic blood pressure. --- ### 2. Confirming the Diagnosis (Out-of-Office Monitoring) If the clinic blood pressure is between **140/90 mmHg and 180/120 mmHg**, do not diagnose hypertension immediately. Offer out-of-office monitoring to confirm the diagnosis: * **Gold Standard – ABPM (Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring):** * Ensure at least 2 measurements per hour are taken during the person's usual waking hours (e.g., between 08:00 and 22:00). * Use the **average of at least 14 measurements** taken during waking hours to confirm the diagnosis. * **Alternative – HBPM (Home Blood Pressure Monitoring):** * Used if the patient cannot tolerate or declines ABPM. * For each recording, take two consecutive measurements, at least 1 minute apart, while seated. * Record BP twice daily (ideally morning and evening) for at least 4 days, and ideally **7 days**. * **Discard the measurements from the first day** and use the average of all remaining measurements to confirm the diagnosis. --- ### 3. Parallel Investigations (While Waiting for Confirmation) While waiting for ABPM or HBPM results, carry out the following for patients with a clinic BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg: 1. **Assess for Target Organ Damage:** * **Urine:** Test for haematuria (dipstick) and send a sample for the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR). * **Bloods:** Check HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine, eGFR, total cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol. * **Eyes:** Examine the fundi for the presence of hypertensive retinopathy. * **Heart:** Perform a 12-lead ECG. 2. **Assess Cardiovascular Risk:** * Use a formal assessment tool (such as **QRISK**) to estimate their 10-year cardiovascular disease risk. --- ### 4. Diagnostic Thresholds & Staging Hypertension is diagnosed and staged using both the clinic reading and the subsequent ABPM/HBPM average: * **Stage 1 Hypertension:** * **Clinic BP:** 140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg **AND** * **Subsequent ABPM/HBPM average:** 135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg. * **Stage 2 Hypertension:** * **Clinic BP:** 160/100 mmHg or higher (but < 180/120 mmHg) **AND** * **Subsequent ABPM/HBPM average:** 150/95 mmHg or higher. * **Stage 3 (Severe) Hypertension:** * **Clinic systolic BP:** ≥ 180 mmHg **OR** **Clinic diastolic BP:** ≥ 120 mmHg. --- ### 5. Special Action for Severe Hypertension (≥ 180/120 mmHg) If a patient presents in the clinic with a BP of **180/120 mmHg or higher**, do not wait for ABPM/HBPM before acting: * **Same-day specialist referral** is required if they have: * Signs of **retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema** (accelerated/malignant hypertension). * **Life-threatening symptoms** (e.g., new-onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury). * Suspected **phaeochromocytoma** (e.g., labile/postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, abdominal pain, or diaphoresis). * **If there are NO symptoms or signs listed above:** * Carry out investigations for target organ damage immediately. * If target organ damage is identified, consider starting antihypertensive drug treatment **immediately**, without waiting for ABPM/HBPM results. * If no target organ damage is identified, repeat the clinic BP measurement within 7 days, or confirm diagnosis using ABPM/HBPM. ``` ::: ::: ## Grounding with `ragnar` & `embed_google_gemini()` Instead of pasting all 52 pages of the NICE guideline into the prompt, `ragnar` chunks the document and uses `embed_google_gemini()` to index each chunk as a semantic vector in DuckDB: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ragnar) library(pdftools) chunks <- pdf_text(nice_url) |> paste(collapse = "\n") |> MarkdownDocument(origin = nice_url) |> markdown_chunk() store <- ragnar_store_create( location = ":memory:", embed = embed_google_gemini() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` duckdb is storing downloaded extensions and secrets under ~/.duckdb: ℹ /Users/orms0426/.duckdb This persists across sessions and is shared with the DuckDB CLI and other clients. ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to use a temporary directory instead. ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ragnar_store_insert(store, chunks) ragnar_store_build_index(store) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_nice_rag <- chat$clone()$set_turns(list())$set_system_prompt("You are an expert clinical phenotyper. Answer strictly using retrieved NICE NG136 excerpts.") ragnar_register_tool_retrieve( chat = chat_nice_rag, store = store, store_description = "NICE NG136 hypertension guideline chunks" ) chat_nice_rag$chat( "According to NICE NG136, what blood pressure thresholds define Stage 1 vs Stage 2 hypertension?" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ◯ [tool call] search_store_001(text = c("What blood pressure thresholds define Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension?", ...) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ● #> [ ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> { ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "origin": "https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213", ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "doc_id": 1, ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "chunk_id": 16, ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> … ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` According to the **Terms used in this guideline** section of NICE NG136, Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension are defined by both clinic blood pressure and subsequent ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) or home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) thresholds: ### **Stage 1 Hypertension** * **Clinic blood pressure:** Ranging from **140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg**, **AND** * **Subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average:** Ranging from **135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg**. ### **Stage 2 Hypertension** * **Clinic blood pressure:** **160/100 mmHg or higher, but less than 180/120 mmHg**, **AND** * **Subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average:** **150/95 mmHg or higher**. *(Note: A clinic systolic blood pressure of 180 mmHg or higher or a clinic diastolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg or higher is classified as **Stage 3 or severe hypertension**).* ``` ::: :::
